title: Molecular Profiling of Spinal Disease Progression in Ankylosing Spondylitis
text:
Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) causes decreased physical functioning and disability due to aberrant bone formation
and damage of the spine. In this proposal we will develop tools that can help prognosticate AS patients’ risk of
severe spinal disease through molecular profiling and biomarker identification. Furthermore, the results will
provide a foundation for studies investigating the pathophysiology of AS spinal disease and enhance
recruitment in clinical trials studying treatments for this disease-specific outcome.

title: Spatial-temporal regulation of physiological stem cell dynamics
text:
Organs are dynamic cellular ecosystems that collectively sense and respond to the organ's
physiological state, but the mechanisms that give rise to their exquisite coordination remain
poorly understood. This research will investigate how the gut precisely couples stem cell
division with cell death to maintain homeostasis, how mechanical stretch from food intake
triggers gut growth, and how supporting tissues coordinate these processes to optimize organ
function. The outcomes of these studies will establish foundational principles for developing
next-generation regenerative therapies to repair damaged organs and improve treatments for
intestinal diseases.

title: Role of HOTTIP/beta-catenin-HOXA9/PRMT1 axis in hematopoietic and leukemic stem cells
text:
Regulation of stem cell self-renewal is critical for tissue homeostasis and disease development and the goal of
this project is to understand the collaborative role of HOTTIP/β-catenin-HOXA9/PRMT1 axis in hematopoietic
stem cell (HSC) regulation and early pathogenesis of AML. Our proposal will characterize the function of
individual components and their crosstalk along the axis in regulating hematopoietic self-renewal. The studies
will provide novel mechanistic insights and potential therapeutic targets for modulating hematopoietic self-
renewal.

title: The Role of DPP in Dental Pulp Stem Cells and its Potential in Tissue Regeneration
text:
The major acidic protein in the dentin matrix is dentin phosphophoryn (DPP). We now propose that DPP can
induce “autophagic” signals in dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs), an important cytoprotective mechanism, in a
calcium-rich intracellular environment to promote differentiation of DPSCs to odontoblasts, to synthesize
dentin. Understanding the function of DPP would help in developing a regenerative strategy to restore the
diseased dental-pulp complex.

title: Combatting AntiMicrobial Resistance in Africa Using Data Science (CAMRA)
text: This research is highly relevant to public health, especially in the U.S., because it investigates the global spread and genetic evolution of antimicrobial-resistant (AMR) bacteria, threats that can rapidly cross borders through travel and migration. By generating critical genomic data and advancing diagnostic and therapeutic tools in Africa, it enhances global AMR surveillance and informs strategies to prevent the emergence and spread of “superbugs” that pose a serious risk to U.S. healthcare systems.

title: Immune Exclusion in Cancer Immunotherapy
text:
In this project we investigate tumor cell-intrinsic p38 MAPK signaling as a new mechanism of resistance to
immune-checkpoint inhibitors. We will address this using large-scale, high-dimensional multi-omics and spatial
data as well as biologic correlatives in pre- and on-treatment biopsies from a human clinical trial combining a
p38 inhibitor and anti-PD1 immunotherapy in head and neck cancer. We will further utilize a combination of
bioinformatics analyses, mechanistic HNSCC syngeneic murine and in vitro experiments to validate our
translational observations. Finally, we will identify and validate additional co-activated immune-resistance
mechanisms to target in combination with p38 inhibitor and anti-PD1 for future clinical trial evaluation.

title: Decentralized clinical trial of contingency management digital therapeutic to treat stimulant use disorder
text:
8. Project Narrative
DynamiCare Health has developed a digital therapeutic to address stimulant use disorder
(StUD) that combines remote substance testing, appointment tracking, self-guided therapy, and
contingency management (CM)—the most effective yet under-utilized treatment for StUD. This
project builds on initial clinical success in pilot testing to conduct a rigorous, long-term,
large-scale RCT to measure clinical impact and cost effectiveness. If successful, this project will
lead to FDA clearance as a medical device and broad payer coverage of a product that could
become the standard of care for StUD and address the national stimulant epidemic.

title: Neurobiology of Cortical Systems
text:
The goal of this project is to provide highly focused and advanced training in the development, function and
dysfunction of the mammalian cerebral cortex at Yale University. Twenty-seven (27) faculty from eleven (11)
basic and clinical departments at both Yale School of Medicine and Yale College are mentors in this
multidisciplinary program for predoctoral trainees. Training includes focused coursework, aggressive mentorship
through advisory committees, intensive research apprenticeship, structured seminar programs, career skills
development, extensive critical evaluation of trainees and the training program, and opportunities for laboratory
and departmental presentations of research progress.

title: Molecular Biology and Cytometry Research Shared Resource
text: MOLECULAR BIOLOGY AND CYTOMETRY RESEARCH SHARED RESOURCE: ABSTRACT The Molecular Biology and Cytometry Research Shared Resource (MBCR SR) is an institutionally managed central core facility that assists investigators in all aspects of research, including initial project consultation, assistance with experimental design, training in protocols and instrumentation usage, sample preparation, data collection and assistance with analysis and interpretation of results. Under the direction of Ken Jones, PhD, the MBCR SR provides six important core services to Stephenson Cancer Center (SCC) members and other investigators: 1) the DNA Sequencing and Genomics Core provides high-fidelity, next-generation nucleic acid sequencing data; 2) the Proteomics Core provides support for biomolecule identification, including complex proteomics analysis, post-translational modification identification, high-resolution molecular weight determination, large biomolecular mass measurements, LC-UV-MS analysis (qualitative or quantitative), protein identification by proteolytic digest (in-gel or in solution), nano LC/MS/MS and database search, and peptide sequencing; 3) the Flow Cytometry and Imaging Core provides flow cytometry and microscopy support for subcellular studies on protein expression, cell cycle and cell signaling; 4) the Cancer Functional Genomics Core provides high-throughput live cell functional characterization of cancer cells, including reverse proteomics array establishment, absolute gene quantification and copy number determination, nucleic acid and protein electrophoresis and imaging, multimodal screening for high-throughput assay on plates, high-throughput, high- content screening of subcellular localized proteins in cells, metabolic analysis of live cells and quantification of clonogenic assay colonies of cancer cells; 5) the Bioinformatics Core provides advanced computational analyses of multi-omic data (Genomic, Proteomic, Metabolomic), and 6) the Mass Spectrometry Core is a nascent core initiated in 2021 as an institutional core specializing in metabolite and small molecule analysis using state-of-the-art mass spectroscopy. This SR has been successful in obtaining funds to purchase metabolomic mass specs for de novo discovery and targeted analysis. The MBCR SR is located in the Stanton L. Young Biomedical Research Center (BRC) on the University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center (OUHSC) campus. This central location provides convenient access to the MBCR SR for the SCC’s laboratory-based members (37 members in BRC, 15 members in the adjacent Biomedical Sciences Building). During the reporting period, 78 full and associate SCC members utilized this facility, with 69 (88%) of these having peer- reviewed grant support. Since this is an institutionally managed core that supports the entire OUHSC campus, it is important to note that full and associate SCC members (n=78) accounted for over a third (35%) of the total users of this centralized facility (n=222). SCC affiliate members (non-CCSG members) accounted for another 27 (12%) of total usage. Combined, these cancer focused members account for by far the largest number and percentage usage by any department or center at OUHSC.

title: Molecular Analysis of Kinetochore Function
text:
The failure to form proper physical connections with chromosomes during mitosis can result in errors
in chromosome numbers or cause chromosome rearrangements. In both cases, these defects are
thought to contribute to tumor progression and birth defects. Understanding the means by which these
units of DNA, and the genetic information that they contain, are properly distributed to new cells is
critical for the diagnosis and treatment of disease. This proposed work will analyze the mechanisms by
which a key cell division structure (termed the kinetochore) associates with both DNA and the rod-like
microtubule polymers from the mitotic spindle that provides the structure and force to segregate the
chromosomes.

title: Automated Quantitative Pathology Imaging and Analysis System
text:
This proposal is to purchase a state-of-the-art automated quantitative pathology imaging and analysis system
as a shared resource for NIH-funded researchers at UW Madison that will replace our currently outdated, end-
of-life high-capacity multispectral imaging system. The requested high-throughput platform effectively acquires
images in multiple modalities, including whole slide scanning to digitize and quantitate in an unbiased manner
protein and nucleic acid-stained tissue slides with high sensitivity and precision to improve the quality and
productivity of the various investigators’ research programs. The acquisition of this equipment will allow the
discovery of several biomarkers of disease in cancer and human development that will impact diagnostic
approaches, treatments, and disease management.

title: Genetically Encoded Probes of Huntingtin Misfolding
text:
The aggregation of the huntingtin protein plays an important role in Huntington’s Disease. This
proposal examines trillions of peptides to find rare molecules that can bind these huntingtin
protein aggregates, but not the rest of the cell’s components, thereby rescuing normal cellular
function. These peptides are designed to have biomarker and therapeutic potential and the
same approach used here can also be applied to other age-related neurodegenerative
diseases, such Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s Disease.

title: Genetically Engineered Mouse Facility (GEMF)
text: GENETICALLY ENGINEERED MOUSE FACILITY (GEMF) The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (MD Anderson) Genetically Engineered Mouse Facility (GEMF) generates customized rodent models for medical research purposes. Cutting-edge technologies (including engineered endonucleases such as TALEN and CRISPR) are used for genome editing and aim at developing sophisticated animal models for the study of human diseases, with a strong focus on cancer. The aims of GEMF are to 1) design and produce genetically engineered animal models through gene modifications; 2) provide quality control on newly generated models (e.g., genotyping, long and short reads sequencing, background characterization, and SNP analysis); 3) provide assisted reproductive technologies (e.g., in-vitro fertilization, cryopreservation, and rederivation); and 4) provide expert advice on colony management and care. GEMF has all the equipment necessary to carry out pronuclear injection of zygotes using plasmids or bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs), targeted transgenesis using embryonic stem (ES) cell injection of blastocysts, or electroporation of engineered nucleases in zygotes, and recently published a key resource paper on the importance of a thorough quality control (QC) workflow (Luqman Front Genome Ed 2025). Using Oxford Nanopore Technologies long read sequencing (LRS) to analyze the outcomes of different Adeno-Associated Virus (AAV) driven integrations, it was shown that unintended on-target mutations (sometimes reported using other workflows) can occur with high frequency. GEMF is a one-stop-shop for all gene editing needs, providing investigators with the latest technological developments in murine genetics, from design to delivery and colony management. During 2024, GEMF supported 42 Cancer Center members (84% of user base), reflecting the critical importance of GEMF services to members. In 2024, GEMF support resulted in 23 publications (48% were in high-impact journals (Journal Impact Factor ≥10)) and facilitated 28 peer-reviewed grants awarded to program members. Future plans include the generation of genetically engineered (GE) mice without the need for vasectomized males, the generation of GE rats, and incorporating innovative new gene delivery methods (e.g., DNA origami) into GEMF services.

title: Epigenetic & Genomics Core
text: A major goal in diabetes research is to understand how alterations in the epigenome and subsequent re- sponses in gene expression impact disease phenotype and treatment regimens. The objective of the Epi- genetic and Genomics Core (EGC) is to provide cutting-edge, reliable and innovative genomic technolo- gies to support the diabetes and related endocrinology and metabolism research goals of DRC investiga- tors. It also offers training, education and consultation in genomics technologies in order to enhance the ability of DRC Investigators to implement these technologies in their research. The EGC will provide the following services: Technical Support For Sequencing-Based Assays: The Core will provide technical support for high- throughput sequencing assays on Illumina sequencing platforms (MiSeq, NovaSeq X Plus), enabling RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), microRNA sequencing (miRNA-seq), Chromatin Immunoprecipitation linked to massively parallel sequencing (ChIP-Seq), Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin with high throughput sequencing (ATAC-Seq), Cleavage Under Targets-based assays (CUT&RUN, CUT&Tag), protein-RNA interactions (CLIP-seq), genome-wide chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C), sequenc- ing of CRISPR Screens and massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs), as well as Whole-Genome Se- quencing (WGS). Single Cell Sequencing Assays: The Core will provide technical support for single cell sequencing as- says, including 10X Genomics Chromium Single Cell Solution technologies, and implementation of new technologies as they arise. Spatial OMICS: The EGC will provide technical support for in situ spatial transcriptomics and protein measurements in tissue sections (spatial OMICS) based on the 10X Genomics Visium HD and 10X Ge- nomics Xenium workflows, as well as implementation of new technologies as they arise. Training and Consultation: The Core will offer consultation and training of students, postdoctoral fel- lows, investigators and technical staff regarding high-throughput sequencing methodologies and data analysis, both in the form of individual one-on-one meetings as well as in a technical seminar series or- ganized by the Core. Bioinformatics Support: The Core will provide bioinformatics support for assistance with experimental design, choice of technological platform, data analysis and data quality control.

title: Flow Cytometry (FLOW)
text: The Flow Cytometry Shared Resource (FLOW-SR) was established in 1984 and has been continuously funded by the University of Michigan (U-M) Rogel Cancer Center (Rogel) since 1988. While FLOW-SR is available to all U-M faculty, it has been heavily utilized by Rogel members throughout its history. It is well recognized that flow cytometric analysis and cell sorting are critical for measuring a variety of cellular biomarkers and processes in cancer-related life science disciplines including cell biology, immunology, biochemistry, genetics, and pharmacology. Thus, FLOW-SR is highly relevant to Rogel Research Programs.

title: Animal & Tissue Imaging Shared Resource
text: ANIMAL & TISSUE IMAGING SHARED RESOURCE – PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT The mission of the Cold Spring Harbor Cancer Center (CSHL-CC) is to unravel the fundamental mechanisms that govern the biology of cancer through collaborative research and technology development while training exceptional cancer scientists to become future leaders in the field. The Animal & Tissue Imaging Shared Resource (ATI-SR) supports that mission by providing CSHL-CC members with comprehensive molecular imaging capabilities for dynamic assessment of tumor biology in vivo and for histological characterization of tumor tissues. The ATI-SR supports research in the molecular drivers of cancer, cancer physiology, cancer heterogeneity, and preclinical therapeutics cross-Programmatic themes that make up the CSHL-CC strategic plan and is critical for the strategic pillar of Catalyzing Fundamental Discoveries in Cancer. Led by Faculty Head Peter Westcott, Ph.D., Director Scott Lyons, Ph.D. (who oversees animal and molecular imaging services), and Manager Kristin Milicich, B.S. (who oversees histology services), the ATI-SR offers access to state-of-the-art imaging instrumentation and specialized expertise. Services extensively used by CSHL-CC members include ultrasound, optical (bioluminescence and fluorescence), PET (positron emission tomography), SPECT (single photon emission computed tomography) and CT (computed tomography) imaging for in vivo visualization, as well as histology services. ATI-SR staff members work collaboratively with researchers to develop novel methods to assess tumor response to treatment and characterize new diagnostic approaches. Comprehensive research support includes experimental guidance, assistance with data analysis, and training through lectures, workshops, and hands-on assistance. In the current funding period, institutional support enabled the acquisition of an Olympus VS200 scanner, Lunaphore COMET platform for multiplex immunofluorescence analysis, specialized ultrasound software, a Nanodrop spectrophotometer, and a small animal image-guided radiotherapy instrument (SARRP, Xstrahl). This new equipment is instrumental to helping the CSHL-CC complete the strategic goal of fostering research that uses spatial biology techniques, which will be supported by the recent addition of human pathologist Zhen Zhao, M.D., Ph.D., who is developing spatial histopathology methods. During the current period, the ATI-SR contributed to 66 publications, including 36 in journals with an impact factor above 10, and 16 (24%) featured ATI-SR staff as co-authors, demonstrating the value they add to CSHL-CC research. From 2021-2024, the ATI-SR was used by 31 CSHL-CC members (54% of members). Usage by CSHL-CC members comprised 94% of animal and molecular imaging services (24 members) and 99% of histology services (28 members). The technical and labor-intensive services provided by the ATI-SR make advanced imaging accessible to investigators who would otherwise be unable to incorporate these analytical workflows into their cancer research.

title: Targeting the metastasis initiating cell in undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma
text:
Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma is a soft tissue sarcoma with one of the worst prognosis.
We identified an innovative approach to treatment based on targeting a small population of
tumor cells that are responsible for metastasis. This proposal will determine how this treatment
approach will best work for patients with this devastating tumor type.

title: Defining and treating genetic abnormalities in psoriasis/atopic dermatitis-overlap dermatoses
text:
The proposed project is relevant to public health because it seeks biomarkers that differentiate complex
inflammatory skin diseases, better directing existing treatments and reducing the expense and morbidity
stemming from failed treatments. Thus, this proposal is relevant to the part of NIH's mission that addresses
technological innovations and clinically directed research strategies as a basis for improving human health.

title: Mechanistic dissection of eukaryotic protein biogenesis and degradation pathways
text:
Our lab studies how human cells help one of their most abundant proteins achieve its correct
three-dimensional shape; this protein enables production of all other proteins and is blocked by a drug with
pre-clinical efficacy against SARS-CoV-2. We also study how human cells adapt to stress by remodeling their
intracellular membrane compartments by a quality control process that staves-off neuronal degeneration with
age.

title: The Regulatory Mechanisms of Osteoclasts
text:
Osteoclasts are the sole bone-resorbing cells. Dysregulation of osteoclasts results in excessive bone loss. At
present, available strategies for the prevention and treatment of bone loss have significant limitations,
rendering prolonged use undesirable. A better understanding of osteoclast regulation will offer new
opportunities for disease prevention.
